# Central Africa Regiment

## Formation and Origins

The Central Africa Regiment (CAR) occupies a significant yet often overlooked position in the history of British colonial military forces in East and Central Africa. It was not a long-standing institution but rather a crucial transitional unit, existing for approximately six years between 1896 and 1902 , . Its primary importance lies in its role as the direct organizational precursor to the 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions of the King's African Rifles (KAR), which would go on to become a major component of the British Empire's war effort in Africa during World War I , , . Understanding the CAR requires tracing its lineage back to its immediate predecessors, the Central African Rifles, and situating its formation within the broader context of British imperial expansion and the consolidation of colonial control in the late 19th century. The narrative of the CAR's origins reveals a deliberate evolution from smaller, locally-raised militias into a more centralized and standardized colonial force, reflecting the administrative trends of the era.

The genesis of the CAR can be traced to the "Central African Rifles," a multi-ethnic military unit formally established by 1896 under the authority of the British Central Africa Protectorate, a territory that would later become known as Nyasaland (modern-day Malawi) , , . This initial force was raised to meet the pressing security needs of the protectorate, which included combating the lucrative but brutal Arab and Swahili-led slave trade, suppressing resistance from various local African polities, securing newly drawn colonial borders, and maintaining internal order during the chaotic period of imperial consolidation , . The organizational structure of the Central African Rifles itself reflected the prevailing colonial approach to military recruitment and command, which often involved grouping soldiers along ethnic lines. By 1896, the Rifles consisted of three companies of Tonga (A, D, E), two of Yao (B, C), and one mixed company of Chewa and Ngoni (F) , . This deliberate ethnic composition was a strategy to manage recruitment and maintain a degree of control over the diverse populations of the region. Each company was meticulously structured, comprising 108 African soldiers, 6 African sergeants, 6 African corporals, one British officer, one Sikh colour sergeant, and several Sikh drill instructors , . This blend of European and Indian non-commissioned officers was common in British colonial armies and served as a mechanism for training and disciplining the locally recruited African rank-and-file soldiers, who were known as 'askari'.

The establishment of this first regiment was followed by a rapid expansion and reorganization of the colonial military presence in response to escalating threats and the perceived need for a larger, more versatile force. In 1898, the Central African Rifles expanded from its initial five companies to eight, a move necessitated by the need to garrison numerous border forts in North-Eastern Rhodesia . This expansion demonstrates a growing commitment to securing the protectorate's frontiers against both external incursions and internal unrest. The strategic environment remained volatile, leading to a further critical development in 1899. That year, a second regiment of the Central African Rifles was raised, specifically for overseas service with enlistments of only three years , . The creation of this second, shorter-term contingent suggests that the colonial administration anticipated the possibility of conflicts extending beyond the immediate borders of Nyasaland and sought to create a reserve force capable of deployment elsewhere in the British sphere of influence in East Africa. This move also highlights the increasing militarization of the region as Britain consolidated its hold over territories like Uganda and parts of German East Africa (modern Tanzania).

The culmination of this evolutionary process occurred in 1900. The two regiments of the Central African Rifles—the original five-company unit and the newly raised second regiment—were amalgamated and renamed the Central Africa Regiment , . This act of recombination and renaming appears to have been a strategic administrative consolidation. It likely aimed to streamline command and control, unify disparate units under a single identity, and prepare them for a final integration into a larger, more permanent imperial formation. This new, unified Central Africa Regiment, now comprising eight companies, represented the pinnacle of its organizational life . However, its existence was short-lived. On January 1, 1902, the CAR was officially subsumed into the newly formed King's African Rifles . This event marked the end of the CAR as an independent entity. The historical record is unequivocal on this point: the formation of the KAR in 1902 was achieved by merging three pre-existing units: the Central Africa Regiment, the East Africa Rifles, and the Uganda Rifles , . The 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions of the KAR, the first two battalions established upon its formation, were directly derived from the personnel and structure of the Central Africa Regiment , , . By 1910, the Central Africa Regiment had ceased to be referenced as an active entity within the colonial military hierarchy, having been fully integrated into the KAR structure . The lifecycle of the CAR—from the distinct Central African Rifles, to a combined and reorganized Central Africa Regiment, and finally to its absorption into the KAR—mirrors the broader trend of administrative centralization within the British Empire, where locally raised militias were gradually consolidated into larger, more bureaucratic imperial formations.

This table summarizes the key stages in the evolution of the colonial military forces that preceded the Central Africa Regiment, illustrating a clear trajectory towards greater size, specialization, and eventual integration into a larger imperial army.

## Structure and Organization

The organizational structure of the Central Africa Regiment was a reflection of the broader principles guiding the formation of British colonial forces across Africa. It was designed to be a locally-recruited, multi-ethnic military body commanded by white British officers, a system intended to project imperial authority while minimizing the cost and logistical burden of deploying regular British Army troops. The CAR's structure was characterized by a formalized chain of command, a deliberate ethnic composition for its enlisted ranks, and a reliance on Indian non-commissioned officers for specialized roles. While detailed muster rolls and pay lists for the CAR are not provided in the available sources, the organizational framework can be reconstructed based on the structure of its immediate predecessor, the Central African Rifles, which evolved into the CAR , . This provides a clear picture of the types of personnel who constituted the unit during its brief existence.

At the peak of its organization, the Central Africa Regiment comprised eight companies . This number represents the consolidation of the eight companies of the original Central African Rifles, which had expanded from its initial five by 1898 . The ethnic composition of these companies was carefully planned and deliberately segregated, a common practice in colonial armies designed to manage recruitment, foster loyalty to specific leaders, and prevent the formation of pan-ethnic solidarity among the soldiers. Each company was largely composed of men from a single ethnic group, ensuring that commanders could draw on linguistic and cultural familiarity to maintain discipline and cohesion. For instance, the companies were designated as follows: Company A, D, and E were composed of Tonga soldiers; Company B and C were made up of Yao soldiers; and Company F was a mixed company of Chewa and Ngoni soldiers , . This structured recruitment policy allowed the colonial administration to tap into different regional pools of manpower while simultaneously creating distinct military units that mirrored the ethnic divisions of the civilian population.

The command and non-commissioned officer (NCO) structure of the CAR was overseen entirely by Europeans and South Asians. At the apex of this hierarchy was the British officer, who held ultimate command of each company. Below the officers were the non-commissioned ranks, which included African sergeants and corporals who were responsible for the day-to-day training, discipline, and welfare of the soldiers . However, a unique feature of the colonial military structure was the prominent role assigned to Indian soldiers, particularly Sikhs, in the NCO cadre. Each company was supported by a Sikh colour sergeant and several Sikh drill instructors , . These individuals were considered highly disciplined and effective soldiers, making them ideal candidates for the demanding role of training and mentoring the African 'askari'. This reliance on Sikh NCOs was a hallmark of many British colonial regiments, including the King's African Rifles, and underscored the racial hierarchies inherent in the imperial military system. The relationship between the British officers, the Indian NCOs, and the African soldiers formed a complex web of authority and instruction that defined the operational capacity of the regiment.

While the exact strength of the Central Africa Regiment is not specified, we can infer its approximate size from the data on its predecessor unit. The Central African Rifles, which formed the basis of the CAR, consisted of eight companies, each comprising 108 African soldiers , . Based on this, the total number of African rank-and-file soldiers in the CAR at its peak would have been approximately 864 (8 companies x 108 soldiers). Adding the commissioned officers, the Sikh colour serjeant, and the African NCOs would bring the total personnel count to just over 1,000. This estimate aligns with the scale of early colonial forces, which were typically small compared to regular imperial armies but were nonetheless formidable instruments of power in their respective theaters of operation. The entire administrative and financial apparatus of these colonial units, including the maintenance of muster rolls and pay lists, was meticulously recorded in London-based archives. For researchers seeking to reconstruct the CAR's personnel, the relevant records would be found in the War Office series WO 16, which covers colonial troop muster rolls and pay lists from 1878 to 1898, though cross-referencing with the Army List would be necessary due to subsequent reforms . Soldiers discharged to pension might also be documented in series such as WO 97, which covers Chelsea Pensioners' service records from 1760–1913 , . These archival trails offer a potential path for uncovering the names and service histories of individual soldiers who served in the CAR, providing a human dimension to its institutional story.

This table details the ethnic breakdown of the CAR's companies, highlighting the deliberate organizational strategy employed by the colonial administration to manage its diverse military force.

## Operational History and Campaigns

The operational history of the Central Africa Regiment, though brief, was marked by active engagement in the violent and coercive processes of imperial expansion. As a colonial military unit, its primary strategic purpose was multifaceted: to suppress anti-colonial resistance from local African polities, to combat the deeply entrenched Arab and Swahili-led slave trade, and to secure the borders of the British Central Africa Protectorate and adjacent territories , . The CAR's campaign history reflects this dual mandate of pacification and economic exploitation, demonstrating its role as a key instrument of British authority. The available sources document several significant military actions undertaken by the unit prior to its absorption into the King's African Rifles, showcasing its capacity to conduct punitive expeditions, engage in large-scale battles, and operate in joint Anglo-Portuguese ventures. These operations were not merely routine patrols but were directed at powerful adversaries, underscoring the tangible impact of the CAR on the political and social landscape of Central Africa in the late 19th century.

One of the most prominent aspects of the CAR's operational history was its involvement in a series of punitive expeditions against local chiefs and kingdoms who resisted British encroachment and sought to maintain their autonomy. These campaigns were part of a broader strategy to establish and consolidate British rule through military force. Documented engagements include operations against Chief Mponda in 1891, Chief Zarafi in 1892, and Chief Makanjira between 1894 and 1895 , . These actions were likely responses to rebellions or acts of defiance against colonial authority. A particularly notable campaign was the fight against the formidable Ngoni Kingdom of Mpezeni in North-Eastern Rhodesia in 1898 , . The Ngoni, a warrior people who had migrated from Zululand, were renowned for their military prowess. The CAR's participation in this conflict, equipped with two 7-pounder guns and two Maxim guns, indicates a significant escalation in the scale of operations and the use of modern weaponry to subdue a determined opponent . These campaigns highlight the CAR's role in quelling organized resistance and facilitating the imposition of colonial governance.

Another critical focus of the CAR's military activities was the suppression of the trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean slave trade, a lucrative enterprise run by Arab and Swahili traders that was a major target of British anti-slavery missions in East Africa. The CAR was actively deployed against these networks, achieving significant successes. One of the most celebrated victories was the capture of the notorious Arab slaver Mlozi in 1895 , . The operation, carried out by a force described as the 'Ever Victorious Army', resulted in the capture of three stockades belonging to Mlozi and his followers . The aftermath of his capture was equally telling of the hybrid nature of colonial justice; Mlozi was tried by a drum court and subsequently hanged, a form of punishment that blended traditional African judicial practices with the authority of the colonial administration . Other operations focused on clearing slaving strongholds around Lake Shirwa in 1896 . These efforts demonstrate that the CAR was not just a tool for land acquisition but also a key agent in enforcing British moral and economic policies, disrupting a major regional industry and freeing enslaved peoples.

Beyond its domestic campaigns, the CAR also played a role in regional security and international diplomacy through joint operations. A significant example of this was a joint Anglo-Portuguese border operation conducted around Lake Shirwa between 1899 and 1900 . Such operations were essential for defining and securing the contested frontiers between British and Portuguese spheres of influence in East Africa. They required coordination between different colonial powers and demonstrated the CAR's capacity for cooperation and its utility in managing complex geopolitical issues. Furthermore, the CAR's involvement in the First Matabele War of 1893-94, although perhaps more associated with the earlier Central African Rifles, points to its readiness for regional deployments . The cumulative evidence from these diverse campaigns paints a picture of a versatile and effective military force. It was adept at conducting asymmetric warfare against tribal opponents, utilizing superior firepower to overcome well-organized resistance, and participating in high-stakes diplomatic-military operations. While the full extent of its service may be obscured by the destruction of government records in Zomba in 1919 , the documented history confirms that the Central Africa Regiment was a vital and active component of the British colonial state in Central Africa for the six years of its existence.

## The Battle Honour 'Ashanti 1900'

The most compelling piece of evidence confirming the Central Africa Regiment's independent existence, operational reality, and substantive military contribution is the award of the battle honour 'Ashanti 1900'. This distinction serves as a crucial anchor point in the otherwise fragmented historical record of the unit. Multiple sources corroborate that this honour was not originally granted to the King's African Rifles but was bestowed upon the wider KAR structure much later, specifically in 1908 . The official rationale for this grant was to formally recognize and commemorate the prior service of the Central Africa Regiment, acknowledging its accomplishments before its amalgamation into the new imperial formation . This act by the British Army's General Staff provides an authoritative and unambiguous validation that the CAR was not merely a fleeting administrative title but a genuine military unit that had already seen active combat in Somaliland under British command . The honour thus refutes any suggestion that the CAR was simply a placeholder name without a meaningful history of its own.

The inclusion of 'Ashanti 1900' on the regimental colours of various King's African Rifles battalions underscores its symbolic and historical significance. Battle honours are prestigious awards that signify a unit's distinguished and memorable participation in a particular campaign or battle. The fact that the KAR adopted this honour speaks volumes about the perceived value of the CAR's early service. The honour appears on the Colours of multiple KAR units, including the 6th (Tanganyika) Battalion and the 11th Battalion, indicating that it was considered a shared legacy of the entire regiment , . The presentation of the 6th Battalion's Colours in 1955 by the Governor and Commander-in-Chief of Tanganyika further cemented this connection, explicitly linking the battalion's proud history to honours earned decades earlier by its predecessors . This adoption meant that the legacy of the CAR's soldiers, who fought and presumably died in Somaliland in 1900, was preserved and celebrated as part of the collective memory of the KAR. It ensured that their contribution was not lost in the administrative merger of 1902 but was instead formally integrated into the KAR's proud traditions.

Analytically, the 'Ashanti 1900' honour is far more than a simple footnote; it is a definitive proof of the CAR's notability and operational credentials. In the context of military history, where lineage and tradition are paramount, the possession of battle honours is a primary measure of a unit's significance. The honour establishes a timeline that predates the formation of the KAR, placing the CAR's active service squarely in the period of intense imperial competition and frontier warfare in East Africa. It validates the accounts of the CAR's campaigns against local resistance and slave traders, suggesting that these were indeed significant enough to warrant formal recognition from the British Crown. For historians and researchers, this single fact provides a robust foundation for establishing the CAR's legitimacy as a military entity. It moves the discussion from the abstract realm of administrative history to the concrete reality of combat and sacrifice. The honour effectively immortalizes the CAR's early service, ensuring that its role in laying the groundwork for the KAR's future achievements is never forgotten. It stands as a testament to the soldiers who served in the CAR, transforming them from anonymous predecessors into the bearers of a recognized and respected military legacy.

| **Battle Honours Associated with the Central Africa Regiment's Legacy** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Honour** | **Associated KAR Unit(s)** | **Significance** |
| Ashanti 1900 | King's African Rifles (in general) | Awarded in 1908 to the KAR specifically to recognize the prior service of the Central Africa Regiment in Somaliland. Confirms the CAR's independent existence and combat experience before its 1902 amalgamation , . |
| Kilimanjaro | 11th Battalion KAR | Part of the WWI campaign in German East Africa. Represents the KAR's major contribution to WWI . |
| Narungombe | 11th Battalion KAR | Another WWI campaign honour from German East Africa . |
| Somaliland 1901-1904 | 6th Battalion KAR | Recognizes the KAR's continued service against Somali rebels after the CAR's disbandment, showing the continuation of the colonial military's mission in the Horn of Africa . |
| East Africa 1914-18 | 11th Battalion KAR | The overarching theatre honour for the entire East African Campaign of WWI, encompassing all KAR battalions' service . |

This table illustrates the hierarchy of honours, with 'Ashanti 1900' standing out as the foundational honour directly linked to the CAR's pre-KAR service.

## Absorption into the King's African Rifles

The dissolution of the Central Africa Regiment in 1902 was not an abrupt termination but rather the culmination of a deliberate imperial strategy to consolidate and standardize the disparate colonial military forces across East and Central Africa. On January 1, 1902, the CAR was officially absorbed into the newly formed King's African Rifles, marking the end of its independent existence and the beginning of a new chapter for its soldiers and officers as part of a larger, more permanent imperial army . This amalgamation was a pivotal moment in the history of the region's military forces, representing the transition from a collection of loosely connected protectorate militias to a unified and centrally administered corps. The process of absorption was methodical, ensuring that the institutional knowledge, personnel, and operational ethos of the CAR were seamlessly integrated into the nascent KAR structure.

The formation of the King's African Rifles was a direct result of this administrative centralization. It was created by merging three distinct and pre-existing units: the Central Africa Regiment, the East Africa Rifles (from Kenya), and the Uganda Rifles , . This consolidation was driven by the need for a more efficient and cohesive military force to administer the vast and strategically important territories of the British East Africa sphere. The KAR was envisioned as a professional, locally-recruited force capable of defending colonial interests, maintaining internal security, and projecting power across a wide geographical area that spanned modern-day Kenya, Uganda, Tanganyika (Tanzania), Northern Rhodesia (Zambia), Nyasaland (Malawi), and even extended into German East Africa and Portuguese East Africa , . The decision to merge these units was a pragmatic one, designed to eliminate duplication of effort, standardize training and equipment, and create a truly regional military power under a single command.

The integration of the Central Africa Regiment into this new formation was direct and foundational. The 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, which were the first two battalions established upon the KAR's creation, were formed directly from the personnel and structure of the CAR , , . Specifically, the 1st (Nyasaland) Battalion was derived from the 1st Central Africa Regiment, while the 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalion came from the 2nd Central Africa Regiment . The 1st Battalion inherited the eight companies of the original CAR, while the 2nd Battalion was formed from the six companies of the 1899-raised second regiment . This direct lineage ensured that the traditions and fighting spirit of the CAR were passed down to its successors. The soldiers who had served in the CAR's campaigns against Mlozi and Mpezeni became the backbone of the 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, carrying with them the experience gained in the harsh realities of frontier warfare. These battalions were tasked with the defense of Nyasaland, a core responsibility that fell to the direct descendants of the CAR . The official designations of the new battalions retained the word 'Central African', serving as a subtle but important acknowledgment of their origins .

By 1910, the Central Africa Regiment had completely disappeared from official military records, having been fully subsumed into the KAR structure . Its personnel were no longer mustered under the CAR's name but were now identified as members of the 1st or 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions of the King's African Rifles. The command structure was also reorganized under the new KAR hierarchy. However, the fundamental character of the force remained remarkably consistent. The KAR continued to be composed almost exclusively of African 'askari' led by white British officers, a model perfected by the colonial militias that preceded it . The soldiers of the 1st and 2nd Battalions, formerly of the CAR, were now prepared for the next phase of their military careers, which would see them play a decisive role in World War I. Their experience in the challenging terrain of Central Africa and their proven ability to conduct sustained campaigns made them invaluable assets. The absorption of the CAR into the KAR was therefore not an end but a beginning; it was the moment the best-trained and most experienced soldiers of the Nyasaland Protectorate were forged into elite components of the greatest colonial army in Africa, ready to answer the call to arms for the British Empire on a global stage.

## Post-1902 Legacy and Commemoration

Since its formal disbandment in 1902, the Central Africa Regiment has existed primarily as a historical concept—a foundational unit whose legacy lives on entirely through the history and commemoration of its successor battalions within the King's African Rifles. The soldiers of the CAR did not disappear from the historical record; rather, they became the ancestors of the askari who fought with distinction across East Africa during World War I. The true measure of the CAR's enduring impact is not found in its own brief operational history but in the monumental contribution of the 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, which it directly spawned, and in the modern, formal recognition of their sacrifices. This posthumous commemoration has transformed the memory of the CAR's fallen soldiers from an anonymous group of predecessors into named individuals with a recognized place in history, thereby completing the story of the unit's legacy.

The most significant chapter in the CAR's post-1902 legacy is its contribution to the East African Campaign of World War I (1914–1918). The 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, born from the CAR, were integral components of the KAR's expansion into over twenty battalions by mid-1916 . These battalions, along with other regional forces, formed the Northern Rhodesia–Nyasaland Field Force, which operated under the command of General Edward Northey , . The KAR as a whole grew to comprise over 35,000 men by the end of the war, the vast majority of whom were African-born soldiers . They fought in some of the most grueling conditions imaginable, battling not only the German colonial forces in German East Africa (modern Tanzania) but also disease, starvation, and the unforgiving terrain. The 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, as the direct institutional heirs of the CAR, participated in these major campaigns, continuing the tradition of frontline service established by their predecessors. Their involvement in the coordinated operations across the German East Africa border and the Lake Tanganyika region solidified their reputation as a tough and reliable fighting force .

For decades, however, the immense sacrifice of these African soldiers was largely overlooked in the dominant narratives of World War I. The story of the askari was often relegated to footnotes, their contributions overshadowed by those of their European counterparts. This historical imbalance began to be corrected in recent years through dedicated research and commemorative projects. The most profound development in this regard has been the formal entry of the names of nearly 1,300 African soldiers who died in World War I while serving in the Malawi-based KAR units onto the Commonwealth War Graves Commission (CWGC) database . These soldiers all belonged to the 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions of the KAR—the very units that were formed from the Central Africa Regiment . The names of these men, who were previously commemorated only on memorials without individual inscriptions, are now officially recorded, ensuring they will not be forgotten. This act effectively brings the memory of the CAR's fallen soldiers back into the public consciousness, honoring the ultimate price paid by the men who served in the unit that preceded the KAR.

This modern commemoration finds its physical embodiment in the Zomba 1914–1918 Memorial Tower in Malawi , . Unveiled in 1924, this unique clock tower memorial was erected by public subscription to honor the askari casualties of the two Nyasaland battalions . In October 2023, following a partnership between the CWGC, the Malawi Defence Force, and the Department of Museums and Monuments, the memorial was formally designated as the official point of commemoration for the ~1,300 soldiers whose names were added to the CWGC records . The octagonal cloister of the tower features brass tablets inscribed with the names of the fallen, creating a lasting tribute to their service and sacrifice . This act connects the legacy of the CAR directly to a modern site of remembrance. It transforms the abstract concept of a "predecessor unit" into a tangible link to the individuals who bore its name in life and whose names now bear witness to its legacy in death. In conclusion, the story of the Central Africa Regiment does not end in 1902. It culminates in this powerful act of historical recovery and remembrance, ensuring that the soldiers who formed the first battalions of the King's African Rifles are finally given the recognition they so richly deserve.

At the peak of its organization, the Central Africa Regiment comprised eight companies.
The eight companies of the Central Africa Regiment represent the consolidation of the eight companies of the original Central African Rifles, which had expanded from its initial five by 1898.

The ethnic composition of the Central Africa Regiment's companies was carefully planned and deliberately segregated, a common practice in colonial armies designed to manage recruitment, foster loyalty to specific leaders, and prevent the formation of pan-ethnic solidarity among the soldiers.

Each company (of the Central Africa Regiment) was largely composed of men from a single ethnic group, ensuring that commanders could draw on linguistic and cultural familiarity to maintain discipline and cohesion.
Company A, D, and E of the Central Africa Regiment were composed of Tonga soldiers.
Company B and C of the Central Africa Regiment were made up of Yao soldiers.
Company F of the Central Africa Regiment was a mixed company of Chewa and Ngoni soldiers.

This structured recruitment policy (of the Central Africa Regiment) allowed the colonial administration to tap into different regional pools of manpower while simultaneously creating distinct military units that mirrored the ethnic divisions of the civilian population.
The command and non-commissioned officer (NCO) structure of the Central Africa Regiment (CAR) was overseen entirely by Europeans and South Asians.
At the apex of the CAR's hierarchy was the British officer, who held ultimate command of each company.

Below the officers (in the CAR) were the non-commissioned ranks, which included African sergeants and corporals who were responsible for the day-to-day training, discipline, and welfare of the soldiers.
A unique feature of the colonial military structure was the prominent role assigned to Indian soldiers, particularly Sikhs, in the NCO cadre.
Each company (of the CAR) was supported by a Sikh colour sergeant and several Sikh drill instructors.

These individuals (Sikh colour sergeants and drill instructors) were considered highly disciplined and effective soldiers, making them ideal candidates for the demanding role of training and mentoring the African 'askari'.
This reliance on Sikh NCOs was a hallmark of many British colonial regiments, including the King's African Rifles, and underscored the racial hierarchies inherent in the imperial military system.
The relationship between the British officers, the Indian NCOs, and the African soldiers formed a complex web of authority and instruction that defined the operational capacity of the regiment.
The exact strength of the Central Africa Regiment is not specified, but its approximate size can be inferred from the data on its predecessor unit.
The Central African Rifles, which formed the basis of the CAR, consisted of eight companies, each comprising 108 African soldiers.
Based on the Central African Rifles' composition, the total number of African rank-and-file soldiers in the CAR at its peak would have been approximately 864 (8 companies x 108 soldiers).
Adding the commissioned officers, the Sikh colour serjeant, and the African NCOs would bring the total personnel count of the CAR to just over 1,000.

This estimate (of CAR personnel) aligns with the scale of early colonial forces, which were typically small compared to regular imperial armies but were nonetheless formidable instruments of power in their respective theaters of operation.
The entire administrative and financial apparatus of these colonial units, including the maintenance of muster rolls and pay lists, was meticulously recorded in London-based archives.

For researchers seeking to reconstruct the CAR's personnel, the relevant records would be found in the War Office series WO 16, which covers colonial troop muster rolls and pay lists from 1878 to 1898.
Cross-referencing with the Army List would be necessary due to subsequent reforms when reconstructing the CAR's personnel.
Soldiers discharged to pension might also be documented in series such as WO 97, which covers Chelsea Pensioners' service records from 1760–1913.
These archival trails offer a potential path for uncovering the names and service histories of individual soldiers who served in the CAR, providing a human dimension to its institutional story.
Company A of the Central Africa Regiment was composed of Tonga.
Company B of the Central Africa Regiment was composed of Yao.
Company C of the Central Africa Regiment was composed of Yao.
Company D of the Central Africa Regiment was composed of Tonga.
Company E of the Central Africa Regiment was composed of Tonga.
Company F of the Central Africa Regiment was composed of Chewa and Ngoni.
The operational history of the Central Africa Regiment, though brief, was marked by active engagement in the violent and coercive processes of imperial expansion.

As a colonial military unit, the CAR's primary strategic purpose was multifaceted: to suppress anti-colonial resistance from local African polities, to combat the deeply entrenched Arab and Swahili-led slave trade, and to secure the borders of the British Central Africa Protectorate and adjacent territories.
The CAR's campaign history reflects this dual mandate of pacification and economic exploitation, demonstrating its role as a key instrument of British authority.

The available sources document several significant military actions undertaken by the unit prior to its absorption into the King's African Rifles, showcasing its capacity to conduct punitive expeditions, engage in large-scale battles, and operate in joint Anglo-Portuguese ventures.

These operations were not merely routine patrols but were directed at powerful adversaries, underscoring the tangible impact of the CAR on the political and social landscape of Central Africa in the late 19th century.

One of the most prominent aspects of the CAR's operational history was its involvement in a series of punitive expeditions against local chiefs and kingdoms who resisted British encroachment and sought to maintain their autonomy.
These campaigns were part of a broader strategy to establish and consolidate British rule through military force.
Documented engagements (of the CAR) include operations against Chief Mponda in 1891, Chief Zarafi in 1892, and Chief Makanjira between 1894 and 1895.
These actions were likely responses to rebellions or acts of defiance against colonial authority.
A particularly notable campaign was the fight against the formidable Ngoni Kingdom of Mpezeni in North-Eastern Rhodesia in 1898.
The Ngoni, a warrior people who had migrated from Zululand, were renowned for their military prowess.

The CAR's participation in this conflict (against the Ngoni Kingdom), equipped with two 7-pounder guns and two Maxim guns, indicates a significant escalation in the scale of operations and the use of modern weaponry to subdue a determined opponent.
These campaigns highlight the CAR's role in quelling organized resistance and facilitating the imposition of colonial governance.

Another critical focus of the CAR's military activities was the suppression of the trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean slave trade, a lucrative enterprise run by Arab and Swahili traders that was a major target of British anti-slavery missions in East Africa.
The CAR was actively deployed against these networks, achieving significant successes.
One of the most celebrated victories was the capture of the notorious Arab slaver Mlozi in 1895.
The operation (to capture Mlozi), carried out by a force described as the 'Ever Victorious Army', resulted in the capture of three stockades belonging to Mlozi and his followers.

The aftermath of Mlozi's capture was equally telling of the hybrid nature of colonial justice; Mlozi was tried by a drum court and subsequently hanged, a form of punishment that blended traditional African judicial practices with the authority of the colonial administration.
Other operations focused on clearing slaving strongholds around Lake Shirwa in 1896.

These efforts demonstrate that the CAR was not just a tool for land acquisition but also a key agent in enforcing British moral and economic policies, disrupting a major regional industry and freeing enslaved peoples.
Beyond its domestic campaigns, the CAR also played a role in regional security and international diplomacy through joint operations.
A significant example of this was a joint Anglo-Portuguese border operation conducted around Lake Shirwa between 1899 and 1900.
Such operations were essential for defining and securing the contested frontiers between British and Portuguese spheres of influence in East Africa.
They required coordination between different colonial powers and demonstrated the CAR's capacity for cooperation and its utility in managing complex geopolitical issues.
Furthermore, the CAR's involvement in the First Matabele War of 1893-94, although perhaps more associated with the earlier Central African Rifles, points to its readiness for regional deployments.
The cumulative evidence from these diverse campaigns paints a picture of a versatile and effective military force.

It was adept at conducting asymmetric warfare against tribal opponents, utilizing superior firepower to overcome well-organized resistance, and participating in high-stakes diplomatic-military operations.

While the full extent of its service may be obscured by the destruction of government records in Zomba in 1919, the documented history confirms that the Central Africa Regiment was a vital and active component of the British colonial state in Central Africa for the six years of its existence.

The most compelling piece of evidence confirming the Central Africa Regiment's independent existence, operational reality, and substantive military contribution is the award of the battle honour 'Ashanti 1900'.
This distinction serves as a crucial anchor point in the otherwise fragmented historical record of the unit.
Multiple sources corroborate that this honour was not originally granted to the King's African Rifles but was bestowed upon the wider KAR structure much later, specifically in 1908.

The official rationale for this grant was to formally recognize and commemorate the prior service of the Central Africa Regiment, acknowledging its accomplishments before its amalgamation into the new imperial formation.

This act by the British Army's General Staff provides an authoritative and unambiguous validation that the CAR was not merely a fleeting administrative title but a genuine military unit that had already seen active combat in Somaliland under British command.
The honour thus refutes any suggestion that the CAR was simply a placeholder name without a meaningful history of its own.
The inclusion of 'Ashanti 1900' on the regimental colours of various King's African Rifles battalions underscores its symbolic and historical significance.
Battle honours are prestigious awards that signify a unit's distinguished and memorable participation in a particular campaign or battle.
The fact that the KAR adopted this honour speaks volumes about the perceived value of the CAR's early service.
The honour appears on the Colours of multiple KAR units, including the 6th (Tanganyika) Battalion and the 11th Battalion, indicating that it was considered a shared legacy of the entire regiment.

The presentation of the 6th Battalion's Colours in 1955 by the Governor and Commander-in-Chief of Tanganyika further cemented this connection, explicitly linking the battalion's proud history to honours earned decades earlier by its predecessors.
This adoption meant that the legacy of the CAR's soldiers, who fought and presumably died in Somaliland in 1900, was preserved and celebrated as part of the collective memory of the KAR.
It ensured that their contribution was not lost in the administrative merger of 1902 but was instead formally integrated into the KAR's proud traditions.
Analytically, the 'Ashanti 1900' honour is far more than a simple footnote; it is a definitive proof of the CAR's notability and operational credentials.
In the context of military history, where lineage and tradition are paramount, the possession of battle honours is a primary measure of a unit's significance.
The honour establishes a timeline that predates the formation of the KAR, placing the CAR's active service squarely in the period of intense imperial competition and frontier warfare in East Africa.
It validates the accounts of the CAR's campaigns against local resistance and slave traders, suggesting that these were indeed significant enough to warrant formal recognition from the British Crown.
For historians and researchers, this single fact provides a robust foundation for establishing the CAR's legitimacy as a military entity.
It moves the discussion from the abstract realm of administrative history to the concrete reality of combat and sacrifice.
The honour effectively immortalizes the CAR's early service, ensuring that its role in laying the groundwork for the KAR's future achievements is never forgotten.
It stands as a testament to the soldiers who served in the CAR, transforming them from anonymous predecessors into the bearers of a recognized and respected military legacy.
The battle honour 'Ashanti 1900' was awarded in 1908 to the KAR specifically to recognize the prior service of the Central Africa Regiment in Somaliland.
The battle honour 'Ashanti 1900' confirms the CAR's independent existence and combat experience before its 1902 amalgamation.
The battle honour 'Kilimanjaro' was associated with the 11th Battalion KAR.
The battle honour 'Kilimanjaro' was part of the WWI campaign in German East Africa.
The battle honour 'Kilimanjaro' represents the KAR's major contribution to WWI.
The battle honour 'Narungombe' was associated with the 11th Battalion KAR.
The battle honour 'Narungombe' was another WWI campaign honour from German East Africa.
The battle honour 'Somaliland 1901-1904' was associated with the 6th Battalion KAR.
The battle honour 'Somaliland 1901-1904' recognizes the KAR's continued service against Somali rebels after the CAR's disbandment.
The battle honour 'Somaliland 1901-1904' shows the continuation of the colonial military's mission in the Horn of Africa.
The battle honour 'East Africa 1914-18' was associated with the 11th Battalion KAR.
The battle honour 'East Africa 1914-18' was the overarching theatre honour for the entire East African Campaign of WWI, encompassing all KAR battalions' service.

The dissolution of the Central Africa Regiment in 1902 was not an abrupt termination but rather the culmination of a deliberate imperial strategy to consolidate and standardize the disparate colonial military forces across East and Central Africa.

On January 1, 1902, the CAR was officially absorbed into the newly formed King's African Rifles, marking the end of its independent existence and the beginning of a new chapter for its soldiers and officers as part of a larger, more permanent imperial army.

This amalgamation was a pivotal moment in the history of the region's military forces, representing the transition from a collection of loosely connected protectorate militias to a unified and centrally administered corps.
The process of absorption was methodical, ensuring that the institutional knowledge, personnel, and operational ethos of the CAR were seamlessly integrated into the nascent KAR structure.
The formation of the King's African Rifles was a direct result of this administrative centralization.
It was created by merging three distinct and pre-existing units: the Central Africa Regiment, the East Africa Rifles (from Kenya), and the Uganda Rifles.
This consolidation was driven by the need for a more efficient and cohesive military force to administer the vast and strategically important territories of the British East Africa sphere.

The KAR was envisioned as a professional, locally-recruited force capable of defending colonial interests, maintaining internal security, and projecting power across a wide geographical area that spanned modern-day Kenya, Uganda, Tanganyika (Tanzania), Northern Rhodesia (Zambia), Nyasaland (Malawi), and even extended into German East Africa and Portuguese East Africa.

The decision to merge these units was a pragmatic one, designed to eliminate duplication of effort, standardize training and equipment, and create a truly regional military power under a single command.
The integration of the Central Africa Regiment into this new formation was direct and foundational.
The 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, which were the first two battalions established upon the KAR's creation, were formed directly from the personnel and structure of the CAR.
Specifically, the 1st (Nyasaland) Battalion was derived from the 1st Central Africa Regiment, while the 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalion came from the 2nd Central Africa Regiment.
The 1st Battalion inherited the eight companies of the original CAR, while the 2nd Battalion was formed from the six companies of the 1899-raised second regiment.
This direct lineage ensured that the traditions and fighting spirit of the CAR were passed down to its successors.

The soldiers who had served in the CAR's campaigns against Mlozi and Mpezeni became the backbone of the 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, carrying with them the experience gained in the harsh realities of frontier warfare.
These battalions were tasked with the defense of Nyasaland, a core responsibility that fell to the direct descendants of the CAR.
The official designations of the new battalions retained the word 'Central African', serving as a subtle but important acknowledgment of their origins.
By 1910, the Central Africa Regiment had completely disappeared from official military records, having been fully subsumed into the KAR structure.
Its personnel were no longer mustered under the CAR's name but were now identified as members of the 1st or 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions of the King's African Rifles.
The command structure was also reorganized under the new KAR hierarchy.
However, the fundamental character of the force remained remarkably consistent.
The KAR continued to be composed almost exclusively of African 'askari' led by white British officers, a model perfected by the colonial militias that preceded it.
The soldiers of the 1st and 2nd Battalions, formerly of the CAR, were now prepared for the next phase of their military careers, which would see them play a decisive role in World War I.
Their experience in the challenging terrain of Central Africa and their proven ability to conduct sustained campaigns made them invaluable assets.

The absorption of the CAR into the KAR was therefore not an end but a beginning; it was the moment the best-trained and most experienced soldiers of the Nyasaland Protectorate were forged into elite components of the greatest colonial army in Africa, ready to answer the call to arms for the British Empire on a global stage.

Since its formal disbandment in 1902, the Central Africa Regiment has existed primarily as a historical concept—a foundational unit whose legacy lives on entirely through the history and commemoration of its successor battalions within the King's African Rifles.
The soldiers of the CAR did not disappear from the historical record; rather, they became the ancestors of the askari who fought with distinction across East Africa during World War I.

The true measure of the CAR's enduring impact is not found in its own brief operational history but in the monumental contribution of the 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, which it directly spawned, and in the modern, formal recognition of their sacrifices.

This posthumous commemoration has transformed the memory of the CAR's fallen soldiers from an anonymous group of predecessors into named individuals with a recognized place in history, thereby completing the story of the unit's legacy.
The most significant chapter in the CAR's post-1902 legacy is its contribution to the East African Campaign of World War I (1914–1918).
The 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, born from the CAR, were integral components of the KAR's expansion into over twenty battalions by mid-1916.
These battalions, along with other regional forces, formed the Northern Rhodesia–Nyasaland Field Force, which operated under the command of General Edward Northey.
The KAR as a whole grew to comprise over 35,000 men by the end of the war, the vast majority of whom were African-born soldiers.

They fought in some of the most grueling conditions imaginable, battling not only the German colonial forces in German East Africa (modern Tanzania) but also disease, starvation, and the unforgiving terrain.

The 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions, as the direct institutional heirs of the CAR, participated in these major campaigns, continuing the tradition of frontline service established by their predecessors.
Their involvement in the coordinated operations across the German East Africa border and the Lake Tanganyika region solidified their reputation as a tough and reliable fighting force.
For decades, however, the immense sacrifice of these African soldiers was largely overlooked in the dominant narratives of World War I.
The story of the askari was often relegated to footnotes, their contributions overshadowed by those of their European counterparts.
This historical imbalance began to be corrected in recent years through dedicated research and commemorative projects.

The most profound development in this regard has been the formal entry of the names of nearly 1,300 African soldiers who died in World War I while serving in the Malawi-based KAR units onto the Commonwealth War Graves Commission (CWGC) database.
These soldiers all belonged to the 1st and 2nd (Nyasaland) Battalions of the KAR—the very units that were formed from the Central Africa Regiment.
The names of these men, who were previously commemorated only on memorials without individual inscriptions, are now officially recorded, ensuring they will not be forgotten.
This act effectively brings the memory of the CAR's fallen soldiers back into the public consciousness, honoring the ultimate price paid by the men who served in the unit that preceded the KAR.
This modern commemoration finds its physical embodiment in the Zomba 1914–1918 Memorial Tower in Malawi.
Unveiled in 1924, this unique clock tower memorial was erected by public subscription to honor the askari casualties of the two Nyasaland battalions.

In October 2023, following a partnership between the CWGC, the Malawi Defence Force, and the Department of Museums and Monuments, the memorial was formally designated as the official point of commemoration for the ~1,300 soldiers whose names were added to the CWGC records.
The octagonal cloister of the tower features brass tablets inscribed with the names of the fallen, creating a lasting tribute to their service and sacrifice.
This act connects the legacy of the CAR directly to a modern site of remembrance.
It transforms the abstract concept of a "predecessor unit" into a tangible link to the individuals who bore its name in life and whose names now bear witness to its legacy in death.
The story of the Central Africa Regiment does not end in 1902.

It culminates in this powerful act of historical recovery and remembrance, ensuring that the soldiers who formed the first battalions of the King's African Rifles are finally given the recognition they so richly deserve.

**[< Africa](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/campaigns/africa/)**

* * *

The campaign in East Africa was a showdown between the British, Belgian and Portuguese Empires on the one side and German Empire on the other. Mainly taking place in German East Africa (modern-day Tanzania), most of the fighting was between black African troops raised in the colonies, led by European officers. The fighting took place over a massive area three times the size of the German Reich.  It was long-drawn-out and extremely costly both in terms of loss of life and use of resources. The death toll was estimated to be 105,000, similar to the number killed in the Battle of the Somme (July – November 1916). However, what made it different from the Western Front was that the majority of the deaths were due to disease, and most of the dead were local people.

### Why did the First World War come to East Africa?

The East African campaign in many ways happened by default, although it is regarded by some as the final stage in the ‘scramble for Africa’. In less than thirty years nearly all of Africa had been colonised by European nations.

[![Image 1](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/East-Africa-Campaign-and-colonial-Africa-272x300.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/East-Africa-Campaign-and-colonial-Africa.jpg)

The East African Campaign and colonial Africa (AFTWF)

At the start of the war German colonies were surrounded by colonies controlled by Entente allies. Germany had grand plans for a huge African Empire (‘_Mittelafrika_’) if it defeated the Allies, as did Britain, running the length of Africa epitomised in the Cape Town to Cairo Railway line.

Far from being an irrelevant sideshow, the East African campaign was for Europe an opportunity to realise imperial ambitions.

[![Image 2](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Ger_claims_Prof_Delbruck_1917-Mittelafrika-Source-Wikipedia-150x150.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Ger_claims_Prof_Delbruck_1917-Mittelafrika-Source-Wikipedia.jpg)

‘Mittelafrika’ (Source: Wikipedia)

As the military historian Harry Johnston put it, _‘the Great War was more occasioned by conflicting colonial ambitions in Africa than by German and Austrian schemes in the Balkans and Asia Minor’_. For the local populations, settler and indigenous, it was another of a string of wars, disrupting the status quo and the challenge of taming the land for mass cultivation along European lines.

### What happened?

At first – as in Europe – the colonists living in East Africa believed that ‘it would be all over by Christmas’, especially as the armies facing each other were tiny – 2400 in the King’s African Rifles in British East Africa and Uganda, and 2700 _Schutztruppe_ in German East Africa. Both forces consisted of black and Arab rank and file. In August 1914, the German occupied the area of Taveta in today’s Kenya and disrupted rail supplies. In November 1914, the British felt in a position to send two Indian Expeditionary Forces to East Africa, one to defend British East Africa (Kenya) and the other to invade German East Africa at Tanga. At this stage, occupation of the German colony would ensure the safety of the Indian Ocean sea lanes for Britain. It was only after 1916, that the desire turned to imperial ambitions.

[![Image 3](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Bundesarchiv_Bild_146-1971-057-05-Tanga-Indian-soldiers-Wikipedia-300x196.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Bundesarchiv_Bild_146-1971-057-05-Tanga-Indian-soldiers-Wikipedia.jpg)

Indian soldiers killed at Tanga, 4 November 1914 (Source: Bundesarchiv / Wikipedia)

Lack of co-ordination (eight government departments), inaccurate intelligence, an underestimation of the enemy’s ability and mismanagement resulted in the 8000-strong invasion force being beaten back by just 1,000 German askaris (locally recruited soldiers). When the British troops sailed off  they left behind modern rifles, 16 machine guns and 600,000 rounds of ammunition, which would be used against them in the months ahead.

The War Office, which had assumed control of operations in the theatre refused to sanction action unless there was a guarantee of success. The British were forced onto the defensive in the north. In the east of the German colony, the Belgians and British were working together to obtain control of Lake Tanganyika which they did when the two British gunboats _Mimi_ and _Toutou_ captured the German _Kingani_ and sank the _Herman von Wissmann_. In the south, the local forces in the Rhodesias and Nyasaland held their own until Edward Northey was appointed commander of the Northern Rhodesia – Nyasaland Field Force and started pushing north into German territory at the same time that the campaign on the British-German East Africa border was relaunched with the arrival of the South African forces in February 1916.

[![Image 4](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Lettows-surrender-November-25th-1918-wikipedia-300x191.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Lettows-surrender-November-25th-1918-wikipedia.jpg)

Von Lettow-Vorbeck’s surrender, 25th November 1918. The picture is revealing: by then, both forces were made up almost entirely of black native troops. The Germans were using pre-industrial transport while the British had been able to bring in some motorised transport. It is also one of the few images from the time by a black African artist. (Source: Wikipedia)

The year 1916 saw an increase in action as the British and Belgian forces forced the Germans into the south-west of the German colony. Portugal officially entered the war in March 1916, having been neutral until then. From late 1916 the war became more mobile with the Allied British, Belgian and Portuguese forces trying to bring the Germans to fight.

In 1917, the Germans moved into Portuguese East Africa before finally returning to German East Africa and then moving into Northern Rhodesia where on 13 November 1918 they were notified of the armistice in Europe. The Germans surrendered in Abercorn (Mbala) on 25 November 1918 and on 19 February 1919 left East Africa to return to Germany.

### Did you know?

[![Image 5](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Battle_of_tanga-painting-by-Martin-Frost-Wikipedia2-300x179.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Battle_of_tanga-painting-by-Martin-Frost-Wikipedia2.jpg)

The Battle of Tanga from a painting by German war artist Martin Frost (Source: Wikipedia)

*   The Battle of Tanga has been called the ‘Battle of the Bees’ because there were numerous bees’ nests in the trees on the battlefield. When the shooting started they swarmed out and stung the soldiers, forcing them back. When combined with fire from the German machine guns, this turned the tide of the battle. In fact the Germans suffered as much as the British from bee stings. Other battles of the bees took place elsewhere in East Africa where hives were prevalent.

*   This was a very multi-national campaign. Only two British regiments were involved. The 2nd Battalion, Loyal North Lancashire Regiment arrived with the Indian Army invasion force at Tanga and after this stayed on the border between British and German East Africa. The 25th Royal Fusiliers (Legion of Frontiersmen) was raised for service in East Africa in early 1915. It served throughout the war. In addition, white contingents were supplied by Rhodesia in 1914 and 1915, the 2nd Rhodesia Regiment, Nyasaland and South Africa including the South African Expeditionary Force which arrived in February 1916. In December 1916 the majority of the white troops were withdrawn to South Africa to recuperate; those fit enough returning to service in East Africa, Mesopotamia or Europe. Most of the Indians returned to India (i.e. India, Pakistan and Bangladesh) whilst some stayed for the duration. From mid-1916, the composition of the British forces changed with the arrival of the Nigerian and Gold Coast (Ghana) contingents and the expansion of the King’s African Rifles from 3 battalions to over 20. The main fighting force now consisted of mainly black African men. In total, it is estimated that 177 micro-nations (tribal groups of all ethnicities) participated in the East Africa campaign.

*   The German cruiser _SMS Königsberg_ was guarding the colony when war began, but it badly needed an overhaul. The crew camouflaged the ship and hid it in the mangrove swamps of the Rufiji River Delta in October 1914. The cruiser was eventually traced and put out of action in September 1915. The 10 guns of the _Königsberg_ and the 6 from the British cruiser _Pegasus_, sunk by the _Königsberg_ in Zanzibar harbour, were converted for land use.

[![Image 6](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/SMS-K%C3%B6nigsberg-in-Dar-es-Salaam-Source-Bundesarchiv-Bild-105-DOA3002-Wikipedia.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/SMS-K%C3%B6nigsberg-in-Dar-es-Salaam-Source-Bundesarchiv-Bild-105-DOA3002-Wikipedia.jpg "The German Cruiser Königsberg (Source: Wikipedia)")The German Cruiser Königsberg (Source: Wikipedia)

[![Image 7](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Shell-craters-by-the-wreck-of-the-Konigsberg-Rufiji-River-July-1915-Bundesarchiv-Source-Wikipedia.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Shell-craters-by-the-wreck-of-the-Konigsberg-Rufiji-River-July-1915-Bundesarchiv-Source-Wikipedia.jpg "Shell craters by the Königsberg, July 1915 (Source: Bundesarchiv / Wikipedia)")Shell craters by the Königsberg, July 1915 (Source: Bundesarchiv / Wikipedia)

[![Image 8](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/German-Schutztruppe-moving-gun-from-the-Konigsberg-Source-Bundesarchiv-Wikipedia.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/German-Schutztruppe-moving-gun-from-the-Konigsberg-Source-Bundesarchiv-Wikipedia.jpg "German Schutztruppe moving a gun from the Königsberg (Source: Bundesarchiv / Wikipedia)")German Schutztruppe moving a gun from the Königsberg (Source: Bundesarchiv / Wikipedia)

*   The search for the _Königsberg_ saw the first use of planes in East Africa. In addition to the hydroplanes used to find the _Königsberg_ and to spot for the monitors (shallow draught gunboats) attacking the ship, two British planes were used by the Belgians to push the Germans out of Kigoma. In 1915, the Royal Naval Air Service introduced aircraft near Taveta which was eventually replaced by the 26th Air Squadron consisting of mainly South African pilots. The 8th Air Squadron was based at Zanzibar. The Germans had one plane which was crashed early in the war.

*   [![Image 9](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/LZ-104-Source-Wikipedia-300x171.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/LZ-104-Source-Wikipedia.jpg)
    
    The Zeppelin L59, later renamed LZ104 (Source: Wikipedia)
    
    In November 1917, the Germans tried to overcome the immensely long supply chain for their troops by sending a Zeppelin from Europe (Bulgaria) to Africa. The huge airship (_L59_) was given a one-way mission. Its canvas envelope was to be used for tents, its metal framework for telegraph masts and stretchers and its leather walkways for boots. It also carried 15 tons of supplies – machine guns, ammunition, food, quinine and other medical essentials. The _L59_ got as far as Khartoum, when it received a message that the German force had moved into the mountains and the airship was likely to fall into British hands, so they turned back. At 95 hours non-stop flying, the journey still holds the record for the longest-ever military flight. The Germans succeeded in getting two ships to break the blockade to East Africa, one of which, the _Kronberg_ was crewed by Danes from Schleswig-Holstein, then controlled by Germany.
    

*   [![Image 10](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/British_motorboat_expedition_1915-Wikipedia-260x300.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/British_motorboat_expedition_1915-Wikipedia.jpg)
    
    The British motorboat expedition, 1915 (Source: Wikipedia)
    
    Lake Tanganyika formed the border between German East Africa and the Belgian Congo, and the German navy controlled the lake with a few small gunboats until December 1915. To win naval control of the lake, allowing Belgian troops to attack from the west, the only way was to carry boats overland. Under the command of the very eccentric Captain Geoffrey Spicer-Simpson, two fast motor launches named _HMS Mimi_ and _HMS_ _Toutou_ were shipped out from Britain and transported overland by train from South Africa to Katanga in the Belgian Congo, including an extraordinary trek which included 146 miles through mountains, using two steam tractors, teams of oxen and hundreds of African porters. 150 bridges had to be built along the way. Eventually, the two boats arrived at Albertville (Lukuga) mid-way up Lake Tanganyika and captured the German gunboat _Kingani_, which Spicer-Simpson renamed as _HMS_ _Fifi_, before gaining control of the whole lake.
    

[![Image 11](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Spicer-Simson-right-on-Belgian-vessel-Netta-on-LakeTanganyika-Wikipedia.png)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Spicer-Simson-right-on-Belgian-vessel-Netta-on-LakeTanganyika-Wikipedia.png "Captain Spicer-Simson on the Belgian vessel Netta on LakeTanganyika (Source: Wikipedia)")Captain Spicer-Simson on the Belgian vessel Netta on LakeTanganyika (Source: Wikipedia)

[![Image 12](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/HMS_Fifi-Wikipedia.png)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/HMS_Fifi-Wikipedia.png "HMS Fifi (Source: Wikipedia)")HMS Fifi (Source: Wikipedia)

[![Image 13](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Geoffrey-Spicer-Simson-in-khaki-kilt-at-left-by-Lake-Tanganyika-1915-Wikipedia.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Geoffrey-Spicer-Simson-in-khaki-kilt-at-left-by-Lake-Tanganyika-1915-Wikipedia.jpg "Captain Geoffrey Spicer-Simson (in khaki kilt, left) by Lake Tanganyika 1915 (Source: Wikipedia)")Captain Geoffrey Spicer-Simson (in khaki kilt, left) by Lake Tanganyika 1915 (Source: Wikipedia)

### Was the campaign different from others?

[![Image 14](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/World_War_I_in_East_Africa-wikipedia-map-240x300.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/World_War_I_in_East_Africa-wikipedia-map.jpg)

The East African Campaign was a war of movement over a wide area (Source: Wikipedia)

It was very different from all the other campaigns of the First World War. Besides covering such a large area, it was a very mobile campaign, with immense logistical challenges and an extremely hostile natural setting. The British could use their naval supremacy to supply their forces and those of their allies, which was not the case for the German army. With depleting forces, the Germans, under the determined leadership of Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, were able to hold on to the end of the war, helped by weak Portuguese resistance which allowed him to resupply at a crucial time. In the few battle encounters such as at Mahiwa, both sides lost significant numbers of their fighting force. Although Lettow-Vorbeck did not succeed in attracting large numbers of fighting men from the Western Front (most of those who fought in Africa would not have fought in Europe) he did succeed in keeping ships occupied and holding the attention of the European war leaders.

### A very hostile environment

[![Image 15](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Kavirondo-BEA-porters-of-the-2nd-Road-Corps.-Chikukwe-Swamp-January-1918-IWM-Q-15625-150x150.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Kavirondo-BEA-porters-of-the-2nd-Road-Corps.-Chikukwe-Swamp-January-1918-IWM-Q-15625.jpg)

Kavirondo (BEA) porters of the 2nd Road Corps. Chikukwe Swamp, January 1918. © IWM (Q 15625)

The East African theatre of war was extremely challenging and the environment was regarded by all as the biggest enemy. Some men wrote home that they would rather be on the Western Front where they could be shot by a sniper than have to deal with wild animals, the weather, jigger fleas and ambushes in grass six foot high. The landscape was undeveloped, with few roads or railways, so the use of wheeled transport was almost impossible and animals such as oxen and mules soon died in the tropical conditions. This meant that all armies relied on huge numbers of porters, initially volunteers but later conscripted. Porters and labour were raised locally, and also came from Sierra Leone, the Seychelles, China and Southern Africa.

### Long lines of communication

[![Image 16](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/British-troops-and-carriers-in-East-Africa-%C2%A9-IWM-Q-15528-300x232.jpg)](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/British-troops-and-carriers-in-East-Africa-%C2%A9-IWM-Q-15528.jpg)

British troops and carriers in East Africa © IWM (Q 15528)

The distances were immense. Supplies were sent from India and Durban, the latter travelling 1,500 miles to the railhead, then transferring to carriers for the additional 450 miles through the bush to the front. To carry just one ton of supplies took 16,500 carriers, and one ton of food was enough to feed the soldiers for one day. In fact, only 2,500 carriers were needed to carry the food for the soldiers; the additional 14,000 carriers had to carry the food for the other carriers! During the campaign, it is estimated that 1 million carriers were recruited, of which, it is believed, a staggering 95,000 died, almost entirely due to poor rations, sanitation and medical care. The medical failings were so concerning – 75% of the armed forces were lost to malaria, dysentery, blackwater fever and malnutrition – that the War Office ordered an inquiry – the Pike Report – which is the focus of our [**Health – The Hidden Enemy**](https://awayfromthewesternfront.org/projects/health-hidden-enemy/) project.

### How did the war affect East Africa?

The impact of the war on the people of East Africa was dire. Many families were affected, either because of involvement in the Carrier Corps or armed forces, or because crops were requisitioned, leading to starvation and poverty; a situation exacerbated by flooding and drought. When famine struck in East Africa in 1917 the civilian population did not have the manpower or food stores to respond; 300,000 civilians died in German East Africa alone. To cap it all, the Spanish Flu epidemic came in 1918, just as the war was ending. In British East Africa alone, 160,000 died – 10% of the population. Ironically, the epidemic would have been much less serious before the war, when African communities were much more isolated from each other; due to the new lines of communication crossing the region, the virus was able to move at devastating speed.

Germany lost the war, and its dreams of an African empire disappeared at the same time, but that was not the end of colonialism in Africa. Britain, France, Belgium and South Africa took over the German colonies. German East Africa became Tanganyika under the British and Rwanda and Burundi under the Belgians. The First World War was instrumental in creating the leaders who led their countries to independence forty years later.

### Further reading

Further detail on the military and social aspects of the East African Campaign can be found in _Paice, E., Tip and Run: The Untold Tragedy of the Great War in Africa (W&N, 2008),_ which has been the main source for this summary.

_Fecitt, H. **[Harry’s Africa.](http://www.kaiserscross.com/188001/home.html)** The soldier’s burden, n.d. \[Accessed 12 December 2024\]_

_**[The Heroes of the East African Campaign of WW1.](https://www.guerrillasoftsavo.com/)** Guerrillas of Tsavo, 2020 \[Accessed 12 December 2024\]_

_Samson A., Britain, South Africa and the East Africa Campaign 1914-1918: The Union comes of Age (IB Tauris, 2005)_

_Jewell, Dr N. P., **[On Call in Africa, in War and Peace 1910-1932,](https://oncallinafrica.com/)** (Gillyflower Publishing, 2016)_ This book contains the story and eye-witness account of events based on the personal diary, memoirs and extensive photography of Dr Norman Parsons Jewell who served as a Medical Officer throughout the First World War in East Africa.

_Moyd, Michelle R., Violent Intermediaries: African Soldiers, Conquest, and Everyday Colonialism in German East Africa (New African Histories) (Ohio University Press, 2014)_ This book sheds light on the German Askari.

The story of Africa’s involvement in the First World War still needs to be published; the main accounts being Eurocentric in approach.

Text by Dr Anne Samson, **[Great War in Africa Association](https://gweaa.com/).**
